questions.q: Which part of a Python traceback should you read first?
options: The last line, which names the error type and reason
The first line, Traceback (most recent call last)
The middle entry, which is always the bug
None of it; rerun the code instead
questions.explain: The final line states the exception and its message; the entries above show the call path, with the most recent call last.

questions.q: int('12.5') fails. Which exception is raised?
options: TypeError
KeyError
NameError
ValueError
questions.explain: The argument is the right type (a string) but its value cannot be interpreted as an integer, which is a ValueError.

questions.q: In a notebook you get NameError: name 'df' is not defined, though you wrote df = ... higher up. What is the most likely cause?
options: Python does not support the name df
You skipped that cell or restarted the kernel without rerunning it
The notebook has too many cells
Assignments only work inside functions
questions.explain: The kernel only knows names from cells that have actually run in the current session.

questions.q: Why is a bare except: (catching every exception) discouraged?
options: It runs slower than a specific except
It is not valid Python syntax
It can hide real bugs; catch the specific error you expect instead
It only works in notebooks
questions.explain: Catching everything swallows unexpected problems silently. Catch specific exceptions like ValueError so genuine bugs still surface.

questions.q: What does assert safe_avg([10, 20]) == 20 do when safe_avg([10, 20]) returns 15.0?
options: Prints False and continues
Stays silent
Raises an AssertionError
Changes the average to 20
questions.explain: An assertion is silent when its condition is true and raises AssertionError when it is false.
